newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hunts oil workers believed kidnapped by rebels.
newsitem.headline: Peru hunts oil workers believed kidnapped by rebels.

text.p: The Peruvian army on Sunday scoured a remote jungle zone in search of about 30 oil workers -- from a local firm under contract to French petroleum company Elf -- believed kidnapped by Maoist Shining Path guerrillas, according to security force sources.
Foot patrols and at least two helicopters joined the hunt in the dense and hilly River Ene zone of Peru's central jungle, where the rebels are thought to be hiding their hostages.
"It's a difficult zone," a military source in the region told Reuters by telephone. "The terrorists have hideouts under the ground, with traps nearby to know when we get close."

The military and other police sources said they received reports from natives in the region that a heavily-armed Shining Path force of between 50 or 60 men captured 29 or 30 workers several days ago, probably on Friday. The workers were apparently employed by local exploration firm Compania General de Geofisica (CGG) under contract for Elf.

"According to the report, the terrorists threatened them. Some of the workers didn't want to go with them, so they beat them," a national police source in the regional capital of Huancayo said in a telephone interview.
A journalist in the zone, who asked not to be identified, said he had confirmed the kidnapping with local natives who witnessed it, local authorities, and civilian self-defense patrols in the area.

The journalist said that, according to those versions, Shining Path had also unsuccessfully tried to capture a CGG helicopter which was about to land at the site of the kidnapping. The self-defense patrols speculated that the guerrillas wanted the helicopter to transport their sick military leader Oscar Ramirez Durand, alias "Feliciano."
An anti-terrorist police source in Huancayo confirmed that 29 or 30 workers had been reported kidnapped, and that army helicopters were searching for them.

"The information we have is that it is Sendero -- the attackers were shouting 'Long Live Sendero' -- although the zone is normally used by the MRTA," he said in a phone interview, referring to Peru's smaller guerrilla movement, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).

The police and military officials said the hostages may include foreigners, but could not confirm this. Elf officials in Peru and France could not be reached for comment, while diplomatic sources in Lima said they had no information.
There was no official confirmation of the kidnapping from the Peruvian government.

Shining Path and the MRTA have been highly active in the dense and isolated jungle area, mainly populated by Ashaninka indians, during a 17-year war on the state. Anti-terrorist police sources have said remnants of both groups -- severely reduced in recent years as a result of a government offensive -- were hiding in the zone.

The MRTA won world notoriety in December 1996 with the kidnapping of hundreds of guests at a Japanese embassy party. They held 72 of their highest-profile hostages for 126 days until Peru's military stormed the ambassador's residence, killing the 14 rebels and freeing all but one of the captives. Two soldiers and a hostage judge also died.

Overshadowed by the MRTA during the hostage crisis, Shining Path had been concentrating on regrouping forces and peasant education work, according to police. The motive for the kidnapping was unclear.

The MRTA's international spokesman, Isaac Velazco, confirmed the kidnapping was not by his group. "In this case, it is not an action by the MRTA, or I would have heard about it," Velazco told Reuters by telephone from Germany. "I know that Shining Path is in the zone. but what could their political motives be? If they are economic motives, they've never done this before."
While the MRTA has been characterized by lucrative kidnappings, the Shining Path has generally raised money from involvement with drug-traffickers.
